arXiv:math/0607708v1 [math.AP] 27 Jul 2006

Long-Time Asymptotic Behavior of Dissipative Boussinesq System

M. Chen1 and O. Goubet2 1Department of Mathematics, Purdue University,
West Lafayette, IN 47907, USA.
2LAMFA CNRS UMR 6140
Université de Picardie Jules Verne,
33, rue Saint-Leu, 80039 Amiens, France.
Abstract.

In this paper, we study various dissipative mechanics associated with the Boussinesq systems which model two-dimensional small amplitude long wavelength water waves. We will show that the decay rate for the damped one-directional model equations, such as the KdV and BBM equations, holds for some of the damped Boussinesq systems which model two-directional waves.

Key words and phrases: 
water waves, two-way propagation, Boussinesq systems, dissipation, long-time asymptotics

1. introduction

Considered here are waves on the surface of an inviscid fluid in a flat channel. When one is interested in the propagation of one-directional irrotational small amplitude long waves, it is classical to model the waves by the well-known KdV (Korteweg-de Vries) equation (see [23])

ut+ux+ux​x​x+u​ux=0,u_{t}+u_{x}+u_{xxx}+uu_{x}=0,

or its regularized version, the so-called regularized long wave equation or BBM (Benjamin-Bona-Mahony) equation,

ut+ux−ut​x​x+u​ux=0.u_{t}+u_{x}-u_{txx}+uu_{x}=0.

When one is dealing with two-directional waves, and the effects of wave interactions and/or wave reflections are not excluded from the study, a restricted four-parameter family of systems (see [5]),

(1.1) ηt+ux+(u​η)x+a​ux​x​x−b​ηx​x​t=0,ut+ηx+u​ux+c​ηx​x​x−d​ux​x​t=0,\begin{split}&\eta_{t}+u_{x}+(u\eta)_{x}+au_{xxx}-b\eta_{xxt}=0,\\ &u_{t}+\eta_{x}+uu_{x}+c\eta_{xxx}-du_{xxt}=0,\end{split}

may be used. The dimensionless variables η⁡(x,t)\eta(x,t), u⁡(x,t)u(x,t), xx, and tt are scaled by the length scale h0h_{0} and time scale (h0/g)12(h_{0}/g)^{1\over 2} where h0h_{0} denotes the still water depth and gg denotes the acceleration of gravity. The variable η⁡(x,t)\eta(x,t) is the non-dimensional deviation of the water surface from its undisturbed position and u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) is the non-dimensional horizontal velocity at a height above the bottom of the channel corresponding to θ​h0\theta h_{0} with 0≤θ≤10\leq\theta\leq 1. The constants a,b,c,da,b,c,d are called dispersive constants which satisfy the physical relevant constraints

(C​0)a+b+c+d=13andc+d=12​(1−θ2)≥0.(C0)\qquad a+b+c+d=\frac{1}{3}\quad\text{and}\quad c+d=\frac{1}{2}(1-\theta^{2})\geq 0.

This class of systems contains some of the well-known systems, such as the classical Boussinesq system (a=b=c=0,d=1/3)(a=b=c=0,\ d=1/3) (see for example [9, 18, 22, 1, 20]) and the Bona-Smith system (a=0,b=d>0,c<0)(a=0,\ b=d>0,\ c<0) [8]. It is shown in [6] that a physically relevant system in (1.1) is linearly well posed in certain natural Sobolev spaces if the constants a,b,c,da,b,c,d satisfy

(C​1)b≥0,d≥0,a≤0,c≤0,(C1)\qquad b\geq 0,\ d\geq 0,\ a\leq 0,\ c\leq 0,

or

(C​2)b≥0,d≥0,a=c>0.(C2)\qquad b\geq 0,\ d\geq 0,\ a=c>0.

It is also shown in [4, 7] that above systems have the capacity of capture the main characteristics of the flow in an idea fluid. But when the damping effect is comparable with the effects of nonlinearity and/or dispersion, as occurs in the real laboratory-scale experiments and in the fields (see [7, 16, 12, 17]), it should be considered in order for the model and its numerical results to correspond in detail with the experiments. The full system would be the Navier-Stokes equations with a free boundary, which is very difficult to handle both theoretically and numerically (cf. [21, 3]). Therefore, it is useful to construct simpler model systems which are capable of capturing the main properties of water waves under various special circumstances.

For example, many researchers have studied the dissipative one-way propagation model equations, such as the dissipative KdV and dissipative regularized long-wave equations and their generalizations. As a model to our study, we recall the results from [2] for the dissipative BBM equation,

ut−ux​x​t−ν​ux​x+u​ux=0,u​(x,0)=u0​(x)\begin{split}u_{t}-u_{xxt}-\nu u_{xx}+uu_{x}=0,\\ u(x,0)=u_{0}(x)\end{split}

where ν\nu is a positive constant.

Theorem 1.1.

Assume u0u_{0} is in L1​(ℝ)∩L2​(ℝ)L^{1}(\mathbb{R})\cap L^{2}(\mathbb{R}), then there exists a constant CC such that

(1.2) ∥u(t)∥L2≤C(1+t)−1/4.\|u(t)\|_{L^{2}}\leq C(1+t)^{-1/4}.

Here L1​(ℝ)L^{1}(\mathbb{R}) and L2​(ℝ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}) are the classical Banach spaces. A similar result holds for the corresponding dissipative KdV equation. See also [7], [15] and the references therein.

In this article, we aim to analyze the effect of dissipation on systems (1.1) and study the decay rates of solutions (η,u)(\eta,u) toward zero. We will restrict our study to the cases where constants a,b,c,da,b,c,d satisfy (C0)-(C1) or (C0)-(C2). The goal of this research is to find the appropriate dissipative term (or terms) which will provide the right amount of energy dissipation for all wave numbers while keeping the mass conserved.

In this article, two kinds of dissipations will be considered:

Complete dissipation: replacing the (00)\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 0\end{pmatrix} in the right-hand side of (1.1) by the vector (ηx​xux​x)\begin{pmatrix}\eta_{xx}\\ u_{xx}\end{pmatrix}, and

Partial dissipation: replace the (00)\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 0\end{pmatrix} in the right-hand side of (1.1) by the vector (0ux​x)\begin{pmatrix}0\\ u_{xx}\end{pmatrix}.

We shall first study the decay rates of solutions to the linearized systems supplemented with either complete or partial dissipations. These equations read

(1.3) ηt+ux+a​ux​x​x−b​ηx​x​t=ν​ηx​x,ut+ηx+c​ηx​x​x−d​ux​x​t=ux​x,\begin{split}&\eta_{t}+u_{x}+au_{xxx}-b\eta_{xxt}=\nu\eta_{xx},\\ &u_{t}+\eta_{x}+c\eta_{xxx}-du_{xxt}=u_{xx},\end{split}

with ν=0\nu=0 or ν=1\nu=1. Systems which satisfy the dichotomy property in the Fourier space:

  • •

    decay as t−1/4t^{-1/4} for low frequencies (small ξ\xi);

  • •

    decay as exp⁡(−β​t)\exp(-\beta t) or exp⁡(−β​ξ2​t)\exp(-\beta\xi^{2}t) for high frequencies (large ξ\xi);

will be identified and studied. It is shown in Section 3 that the dichotomy property will lead to the decay rate t−14t^{-\frac{1}{4}} for ‖(η,u)‖L2×Hh\|(\eta,u)\|_{L^{2}\times H^{h}} (hh will be specified later).

For later use, we shall emphasize (and it is easy to check) that the dichotomy property holds true for two fundamentally different equations: the linearized BBM-Burgers equation ut−ux​x​t+ux−ux​x=0u_{t}-u_{xxt}+u_{x}-u_{xx}=0 and the linearized KdV-Burgers equation ut+ux​x​x+ux−ux​x=0u_{t}+u_{xxx}+u_{x}-u_{xx}=0. If the high frequency part of the solution to a system is damped as exp(−β​t)(-\beta t), we say that the system belongs to the BBM-Burgers class since solutions to linearized BBM-Burgers equation feature this property. If the high frequency part of the solution is damped as exp(−β​ξ2​t)(-\beta\xi^{2}t), which is the case for linearized KdV-Burgers equation, then we say that the system belongs to the KdV-Burgers class. The low frequency parts of the solutions to the linearized BBM-Burgers and KdV-Burgers equations behave in a similar fashion.

The main result in Section 3 is to classify the linearized systems according to this property and to prove that for systems which satisfy the dichotomy property, a decay rate comparing to (1.2) is valid. We shall also present some systems where the decay rates can be arbitrarily small, behaving as the solution of

ut−ux​x​t+u=0,u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x),u_{t}-u_{xxt}+u=0,\quad u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),

where by Fourier transform,

u^​(t,ξ)=e−t1+ξ2​u^0​(ξ),\widehat{u}(t,\xi)=e^{-\frac{t}{1+\xi^{2}}}\widehat{u}_{0}(\xi),

and therefore ∥u(.,t)∥L2\|u(.,t)\|_{L^{2}} could decay arbitrarily slow.

In Section 4, we extend the linear theory to nonlinear systems and show that the decay rate as (1.2) is valid for weakly dispersive systems, i.e. systems with b>0b>0 and d>0d>0, and for some systems in the KdV-Burgers class with total dissipation, which include the KdV-KdV system (a=c=16,b=d=0a=c=\frac{1}{6},b=d=0), with small initial data. In Section 5, the decay rate with respect to L∞L^{\infty}-norm is presented and in Section 6, spectral method is used on several systems to demonstrate that the rates obtained in Section 4 and Section 5 are sharp and the constants involved in the bounds are reasonably sized.

It is worth to note that there are other methods, such as the energy methods (like the so-called Schonbek’s splitting method applied to the classical Boussinesq system [19] in large dimensions), can be used in proving decay rate for solutions of these systems. This line of study will be carried elsewhere. We believe that those methods will be helpful especially in the cases when b=db=d so some Hamiltonian is conserved (see [6]).

On the other hand, to remove the smallness assumption on the initial data, the authors in [2] used a kind of Cole–Hopf transformation (that is valid for Burgers equation) and were able to control the extra-terms. We do not know if this tour de force (feat of skill) is possible for the systems in (1.1) with dissipation.

We complete this introduction by introducing some notations. Throughout the paper, the standard notation on Sobolev spaces will be used. The Lp​(ℝ)L^{p}(\mathbb{R}) norm will be denoted as ∥⋅∥Lp\|\cdot\|_{L^{p}} for 1≤p≤∞1\leq p\leq\infty and the HsH^{s} norm will be denoted as ∥⋅∥Hs\|\cdot\|_{H^{s}}. When several variables are involved, we may also set LxpL^{p}_{x} for Lp​(ℝ)L^{p}(\mathbb{R}) to specify that we compute the norm with respect to the xx-variable. The product space X×XX\times X will be abbreviated by XX and a function 𝐟=(f1,f2){\bf f}=(f_{1},f_{2}) in XX carries the norm

‖𝐟‖X=(‖f1‖X2+‖f2‖X2)12.\|{\bf f}\|_{X}=\left(\|f_{1}\|_{X}^{2}+\|f_{2}\|_{X}^{2}\right)^{{1\over 2}}.

The Euclidean norm of a vector is denoted by |⋅||\cdot|. We will use CC and β\beta as generic positive constants whose values may change with each appearance. Fourier transform of a function ff is denoted by either f^\widehat{f} or ℱ⁡(f)\mathcal{F}(f).

2. Notations and Preparations

2.1. Some notations

Consider ν∈{0,1}\nu\in\{0,1\}. As stated before, we plan to first estimate the decay rates of solutions to the linear systems

(2.1) ηt+ux+a​ux​x​x−b​ηx​x​t=ν​ηx​x,ut+ηx+c​ηx​x​x−d​ux​x​t=ux​x,\begin{split}&\eta_{t}+u_{x}+au_{xxx}-b\eta_{xxt}=\nu\eta_{xx},\\ &u_{t}+\eta_{x}+c\eta_{xxx}-du_{xxt}=u_{xx},\end{split}

when tt goes to +∞+\infty.

Following [6], we introduce the Fourier multipliers

ω1=1−a​ξ21+b​ξ2 and ω2=1−c​ξ21+d​ξ2.\omega_{1}={1-a\xi^{2}\over 1+b\xi^{2}}\quad\text{ and }\quad\omega_{2}={1-c\xi^{2}\over 1+d\xi^{2}}.

Since a,b,c,da,b,c,d satisfy (C1) or (C2), ω1​ω2\omega_{1}\omega_{2} is nonnegative and we denote

H^=(ω1ω2)1/2​ and σ=(ω1​ω2)1/2,\widehat{H}=\left({\omega_{1}\over\omega_{2}}\right)^{1/2}\text{ and }\quad\sigma=(\omega_{1}\omega_{2})^{1/2},

with the conventional notation 00=1{0\over 0}=1. We also denote

α=ξ21+b​ξ2andε=ξ21+d​ξ2.\alpha={\xi^{2}\over 1+b\xi^{2}}\quad\text{and}\quad\varepsilon=\displaystyle{\xi^{2}\over 1+d\xi^{2}}.
Remark 2.1.

When a system satisfying (C2) assumption is the subject of the study, ω1\omega_{1} and ω2\omega_{2} do change signs, but ω1​ω2≥0\omega_{1}\omega_{2}\geq 0.

Definition 2.2.

Consider a nonnegative function ξ→κ^​(ξ)\xi\to\hat{\kappa}(\xi). The order of κ^\widehat{\kappa} (when it exists) is defined as the number mm such that

κ^​(ξ)∼C​|ξ|m\widehat{\kappa}(\xi)\sim C|\xi|^{m}

when |ξ|→+∞|\xi|\to+\infty. The (pseudo–differential) operator κ\kappa with order mm is defined by setting

κ​u=v iff κ^​u^=v^.\kappa u=v\quad\text{ iff }\quad\widehat{\kappa}\widehat{u}=\widehat{v}.

Therefore κ\kappa maps Lx2L^{2}_{x} into Hx−order​(κ)H_{x}^{-\text{order}(\kappa)} (or HxnH^{n}_{x} into Hxn−order​(κ)H_{x}^{n-\text{order}(\kappa)}).

Since (2.1) is a linear system, it is convenient to use the Fourier transform. Let (η^,u^)(\widehat{\eta},\widehat{u}) denote the Fourier transform of (η,u)(\eta,u) and set Y^=(η^,w^){\widehat{Y}}=(\widehat{\eta},\widehat{w}) with w^=H^​u^\widehat{w}=\widehat{H}\widehat{u}, then (2.1) reads

(2.2) Y^t+A​Y^=0,{\widehat{Y}}_{t}+A{\widehat{Y}}=0,

where

A⁡(ξ)=(ν​αi​sgn​(ω1)​ξ​σi​sgn​(ω2)​ξ​σε)A(\xi)=\begin{pmatrix}\nu\alpha&i\,{\rm sgn}(\omega_{1})\xi\sigma\\ i\,{\rm sgn}(\omega_{2})\xi\sigma&\varepsilon\end{pmatrix}

is the symbol of the linear (unbounded) operator in (2.1). Since we are dealing with a system, A⁡(ξ)A(\xi) is a matrix.

By multiplying Y^∗{\widehat{Y}}^{*} on (2.2) and taking the real part,

(2.3) 12​dd​t​∫(|η^​(t,ξ)|2+|w^​(t,ξ)|2)​𝑑ξ+ν∫α(ξ)|η^(t,ξ)|2dξ+∫ε(ξ)|w^(t,ξ)|2dξ=0.\begin{split}&{1\over 2}{d\over dt}\int(|\widehat{\eta}(t,\xi)|^{2}+|\widehat{w}(t,\xi)|^{2})d\xi\\ &+\nu\int\alpha(\xi)|\widehat{\eta}(t,\xi)|^{2}d\xi+\int\varepsilon(\xi)|\widehat{w}(t,\xi)|^{2}d\xi=0.\end{split}

Since α⁡(ξ)\alpha(\xi) and ε⁡(ξ)\varepsilon(\xi) are positive,

(2.4) E⁡(t):=∫ℝ|Y^​(t,ξ)|2​𝑑ξE(t):=\int_{\mathbb{R}}|{\widehat{Y}}(t,\xi)|^{2}d\xi

decays towards 00 as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty, where |Y^|=(|η^|2+|w^|2)1/2|{\widehat{Y}}|=(|\widehat{\eta}|^{2}+|\widehat{w}|^{2})^{1/2} is the Euclidean norm on ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}.

2.2. Linear algebra

We recall some facts from linear algebra and then apply them to the dissipative systems (2.1).

Definition 2.3.

Let MM be a 2×22\times 2 matrix in the complex space, the norm of MM is defined by

‖M‖=supY∈ℂ2\{0}|M​Y||Y|.\|M\|=\sup_{Y\in\mathbb{C}^{2}\backslash\{0\}}\ {|MY|\over|Y|}.
Lemma 2.4.

Let ρ⁡(M)\rho{(M)} denote the spectral radius of a matrix MM and tr⁡(M)\rm tr(M) denote the trace of MM, then

‖M‖=ρ​(M∗​M)1/2≤tr​(M∗​M)1/2.\|M\|=\rho{(M^{*}M)^{1/2}}\leq\rm tr{(M^{*}M)}^{1/2}.

We are now going to bound E⁡(t)E(t) (see (2.2) and (2.4)) by using the pointwise estimate

(2.5) |Y^​(t,ξ)|≤‖e−t​A‖​|Y^0​(ξ)|.|{\widehat{Y}}(t,\xi)|\leq\|e^{-tA}\|\ |{\widehat{Y}}_{0}(\xi)|.

Noticing that the matrix AA can be written as A=D+UA=D+U, where D=(ν​α00ε)D=\begin{pmatrix}\nu\alpha&0\\ 0&\varepsilon\end{pmatrix} represents the dissipation terms and U=(0i​sgn​(ω1)​ξ​σi​sgn​(ω2)​ξ​σ0)U=\begin{pmatrix}0&i{\rm sgn}(\omega_{1})\xi\sigma\\ i{\rm sgn}(\omega_{2})\xi\sigma&0\end{pmatrix} is skew-symmetric. When DD and UU commute, the behavior of ‖e−t​A‖\|e^{-tA}\| with respect to ξ\xi is characterized by the behaviors of ε\varepsilon and α\alpha via

(2.6) ‖e−t​A‖≤e−t​min⁡{ν​α​(ξ),ε⁡(ξ)}.\|e^{-tA}\|\leq e^{-t\min\{\nu\alpha(\xi),{\varepsilon}(\xi)\}}.

But when DD and UU do not commute, more accurate estimate than (2.6) can be obtained by studying e−t​Ae^{-tA} in detail.

We now recall the following lemma (Theorem 9.28 from [13]).

Lemma 2.5.

There exists a unitary matrix QQ (i.e. Q​Q∗=Q∗​Q=IQQ^{*}=Q^{*}Q=I) such that

A=Q∗​(λ1z0λ2)​Q,A=Q^{*}\begin{pmatrix}\lambda_{1}&z\\ 0&\lambda_{2}\end{pmatrix}Q,

where λ1\lambda_{1} and λ2\lambda_{2} are the eigenvalues of AA, ordered by Re​(λ1)≤Re​(λ2)\text{Re}(\lambda_{1})\leq\text{Re}(\lambda_{2}).

As a consequence, one can prove (which is given at the end of this subsection)

Lemma 2.6.

There exists C>0C>0 such that

(2.7) ‖exp⁡(−t​A)‖≤C⁡(1+|z|​min⁡(t,1|λ2−λ1|))​exp⁡(−t​Re​(λ1)).\|\exp(-tA)\|\leq C\left(1+|z|\min\left(t,\frac{1}{|\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{1}|}\right)\right)\exp(-t\text{Re}(\lambda_{1})).

It is easy to see that λ1\lambda_{1} and λ2\lambda_{2} are the roots of the characteristic equation

(2.8) λ2−tr⁡(A)​λ+det(A)=0\lambda^{2}-\rm tr(A)\lambda+\det(A)=0

where

(2.9) tr⁡(A)=λ1+λ2=ν​α+ε≥0\rm tr(A)=\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}=\nu\alpha+\varepsilon\geq 0

and

(2.10) det(A)=λ1​λ2=ν​α​ε+ξ2​σ2≥0.\det(A)=\lambda_{1}\lambda_{2}=\nu\alpha\varepsilon+\xi^{2}\sigma^{2}\geq 0.

We now estimate ‖exp⁡(−t​A)‖\|\exp(-tA)\| by separating the cases Δ≤0\Delta\leq 0 and Δ>0\Delta>0 where Δ\Delta is the determinant of (2.8), namely

(2.11) Δ=tr​(A)2−4​det(A)=(ε−ν​α)2−4​ξ2​σ2.\Delta=\rm tr(A)^{2}-4\det(A)=(\varepsilon-\nu\alpha)^{2}-4\xi^{2}\sigma^{2}.
Lemma 2.7.

For any t>0t>0 and for any ξ∈ℝ\xi\in\mathbb{R},

∙\bullet when Δ≤0\Delta\leq 0 (perturbation range),

(2.12) ‖exp⁡(−t​A)‖≤C⁡(1+tr⁡(A)​t)​exp⁡(−tr⁡(A)2​t)≤C​exp⁡(−tr⁡(A)4​t);\|\exp(-tA)\|\leq C(1+\rm tr(A)t)\exp\left(-{\rm tr(A)\over 2}\ t\right)\leq C\exp\left(-{\rm tr(A)\over 4}\ t\right);

(2.13) ‖exp⁡(−t​A)‖≤C⁡(1+2​|ξ|​σ​min⁡(t,1Δ))​exp⁡(−t​λ1),\|\exp(-tA)\|\leq C\left(1+2|\xi|\sigma\min\left(t,\frac{1}{\sqrt{\Delta}}\right)\right)\exp(-t\lambda_{1}),

where λ1\lambda_{1} satisfies

(2.14) det(A)tr⁡(A)≤λ1≤min⁡(tr⁡(A),2​det(A)tr⁡(A)).{\det(A)\over\rm tr(A)}\leq\lambda_{1}\leq\min\left(\rm tr(A),{2\det(A)\over\rm tr(A)}\right).

Proof.  It is worth to note from Lemma 2.5 that

(2.15) tr⁡(A∗​A)=|λ1|2+|λ2|2+|z|2=ν2​α2+ε2+2​ξ2​σ2.\rm tr(A^{*}A)=|\lambda_{1}|^{2}+|\lambda_{2}|^{2}+|z|^{2}=\nu^{2}\alpha^{2}+\varepsilon^{2}+2\xi^{2}\sigma^{2}.

When Δ≤0\Delta\leq 0 (perturbation range): matrix AA has two conjugate complex eigenvalues λ1\lambda_{1} and λ2\lambda_{2} with

|λ1|=|λ2|,Re​(λ1)=Re​(λ2)=tr⁡(A)2,|λ1|2=|λ2|2=det(A).|\lambda_{1}|=|\lambda_{2}|,\quad\text{Re}(\lambda_{1})=\text{Re}(\lambda_{2})=\frac{\rm tr(A)}{2},\quad|\lambda_{1}|^{2}=|\lambda_{2}|^{2}=\det(A).

Using (2.15) and then (2.10)-(2.9) leads to

|z|2=ν2​α2+ε2+2​ξ2​σ2−2​|λ1|2=ν2​α2+ε2+2​ξ2​σ2−2​det(A)=(ν​α−ε)2≤tr​(A)2.\begin{split}|z|^{2}&=\nu^{2}\alpha^{2}+\varepsilon^{2}+2\xi^{2}\sigma^{2}-2|\lambda_{1}|^{2}\\ &=\nu^{2}\alpha^{2}+\varepsilon^{2}+2\xi^{2}\sigma^{2}-2\det(A)=(\nu\alpha-\varepsilon)^{2}\leq\rm tr(A)^{2}.\end{split}

Hence (2.12) follows from Lemma 2.6.

When Δ>0\Delta>0 (non-perturbation range): tr⁡(A)≥0\rm tr(A)\geq 0 and det(A)≥0\det(A)\geq 0 imply that the matrix AA features two real eigenvalues 0≤λ1<λ20\leq\lambda_{1}<\lambda_{2}. Then (2.15) leads to

|z|2=ν2​α2+ε2+2​ξ2​σ2−tr​(A)2+2​det(A)=4​ξ2​σ2|z|^{2}=\nu^{2}\alpha^{2}+\varepsilon^{2}+2\xi^{2}\sigma^{2}-\rm tr(A)^{2}+2\det(A)=4\xi^{2}\sigma^{2}

and (2.13) is proved by using Lemma 2.6. Since λ2≤tr⁡(A)≤2​λ2\lambda_{2}\leq\rm tr(A)\leq 2\lambda_{2}, one sees immediately that

det(A)tr⁡(A)≤λ1=det(A)λ2≤2​det(A)tr⁡(A){\det(A)\over\rm tr(A)}\leq\lambda_{1}=\frac{\det(A)}{\lambda_{2}}\leq{2\det(A)\over\rm tr(A)}

and (2.14) follows. □\square

It is noted that when Δ≤0\Delta\leq 0, the dissipation can be considered as a perturbation term with respect to the skew symmetric operator. More precisely, the decay is the same as pretending UU and DD commute, up to a linear correction.

When Δ>0\Delta>0, this is no longer valid. In the first case, matrix AA has conjugate complex eigenvalues. In the latter case, AA has real positive eigenvalues and the smallest one monitors the decay estimate. Δ=0\Delta=0 is the bifurcation point.

For the sake of completeness, we now give the proof of Lemma 2.6.

Proof of Lemma 2.6.  Straightforward computations lead to

e−t​A=Q∗​(e−t​λ1z​e−t​λ1−e−t​λ2λ1−λ20e−t​λ2)​Q,e^{-tA}=Q^{*}\begin{pmatrix}e^{-t\lambda_{1}}&z{e^{-t\lambda_{1}}-e^{-t\lambda_{2}}\over\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2}}\\ 0&e^{-t\lambda_{2}}\end{pmatrix}Q,

where

e−t​λ1−e−t​λ2λ1−λ2=−t​e−t​λ2,ifλ1=λ2.{e^{-t\lambda_{1}}-e^{-t\lambda_{2}}\over\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2}}=-te^{-t\lambda_{2}},\quad\text{if}\quad\lambda_{1}=\lambda_{2}.

Lemma 2.4 then yields

(2.16) ‖e−t​A‖2≤tr⁡(e−tA∗​e−tA)=e−2​t​R​e​(λ1)+e−2​t​R​e​(λ2)+|z|2​|e−t​λ1−e−t​λ2λ1−λ2|2.\begin{split}\|e^{-tA}\|^{2}&\leq\rm tr(e^{-tA^{*}}e^{-tA})\\ &=e^{-2tRe(\lambda_{1})}+e^{-2tRe(\lambda_{2})}+|z|^{2}\bigg|{e^{-t\lambda_{1}}-e^{-t\lambda_{2}}\over\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2}}\bigg|^{2}.\end{split}

Therefore, if |λ1−λ2|>0|\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2}|>0

‖e−t​A‖2≤(2+|z|2|λ1−λ2|2)​e−2​t​R​e​(λ1)\|e^{-tA}\|^{2}\leq(2+\frac{|z|^{2}}{|\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2}|^{2}})e^{-2tRe(\lambda_{1})}

which proves part of the lemma.

Now, for |λ1−λ2|≥Λ|\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2}|\geq\Lambda, where Λ>0\Lambda>0 will be chosen later,

(2.17) |e−t​λ1−e−t​λ2||λ1−λ2|≤2Λ​e−t​R​e​(λ1);{|e^{-t\lambda_{1}}-e^{-t\lambda_{2}}|\over|\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2}|}\leq{2\over\Lambda}e^{-tRe(\lambda_{1})};

and for |λ1−λ2|≤Λ|\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2}|\leq\Lambda, using |eζ−1|≤|ζ|​exp⁡(|ζ|)|e^{\zeta}-1|\leq|\zeta|\exp(|\zeta|) for any complex number ζ\zeta,

(2.18) |e−t​λ1−e−t​λ2|=e−t​Re​(λ1)​|e−t⁡(λ2−λ1)−1|≤e−t​Re​(λ1)​t​|λ2−λ1|​et​Λ.\begin{split}|e^{-t\lambda_{1}}-e^{-t\lambda_{2}}|&=e^{-t\text{Re}(\lambda_{1})}|e^{-t(\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{1})}-1|\\ &\leq e^{-t\text{Re}(\lambda_{1})}t|\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{1}|e^{t\Lambda}.\end{split}

Therefore, choosing Λ=1t\Lambda=\displaystyle{1\over t} in (2.17) and (2.18),

|e−t​λ1−e−t​λ2||λ1−λ2|≤C​t​e−t​R​e​(λ1).{|e^{-t\lambda_{1}}-e^{-t\lambda_{2}}|\over|\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2}|}\leq Cte^{-tRe(\lambda_{1})}.

Substituting above into (2.16) completes the proof. □\square

3. Decay rate of linear systems

In subsections 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3, low-frequency (|ξ||\xi| close to 00), high-frequency (large |ξ||\xi|) and middle range frequency analysis for the linear systems are performed respectively. We will identify systems for which there exist positive constants β\beta and δm\delta_{m} such that for any t>0t>0 and

(3.1) ∙ for |ξ|≤δm,∥exp(−tA)∥≤Cexp(−βtξ2),∙ for |ξ|>δm,∥exp(−tA)∥≤Cexp(−βt).\begin{split}\bullet&\text{ for }|\xi|\leq\delta_{m},\ \|\exp(-tA)\|\leq C\exp(-\beta t\xi^{2}),\\ \bullet&\text{ for }|\xi|>\delta_{m},\ \|\exp(-tA)\|\leq C\exp(-\beta t).\end{split}

Here ‖exp⁡(−t​A)‖\|\exp(-tA)\| is the norm of the linear operator exp⁡(−t​A​(ξ))\exp(-tA(\xi)) acting on ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}. The generic constants CC and β\beta are independent of tt and ξ\xi. If δm=+∞\delta_{m}=+\infty is feasible in (3.1), the system is in the KdV–Burgers class. Otherwise the system is in the BBM–Burgers class. A summary of decay rates for the linear systems is given in subsection 3.4.

Remark 3.1.

It is worth to note that (3.1) is sufficient but not necessary for proving the desired decay rate. An example is given in Section 3.3 where (3.1) is not valid but the linear system has the desired decay rate.

3.1. Low frequency analysis

We now prove that for |ξ|→0|\xi|\to 0, all systems are equivalent. This is to say

Proposition 3.2.

There exists positive constants δm,β\delta_{m},\beta and CC depending on the data a,b,c,da,b,c,d and ν\nu, such that for |ξ|≤δm|\xi|\leq\delta_{m} and for any t>0t>0,

(3.2) ‖exp⁡(−t​A)‖≤C​exp⁡(−β​ξ2​t).\|\exp(-tA)\|\leq C\exp(-\beta\xi^{2}t).

Consequently, for any initial data Y0Y_{0} with supp​(Y^0)⊂[−δm,δm]\text{supp}(\widehat{Y}_{0})\subset[-\delta_{m},\delta_{m}],

E(t)≤Ct−1/2∥Y0∥Lx12.E(t)\leq C\ t^{-1/2}\|Y_{0}\|^{2}_{L^{1}_{x}}.

Proof.  By referring to the definitions of Δ\Delta, α\alpha and ε\varepsilon, one sees that as |ξ|→0|\xi|\rightarrow 0,

Δ∼−4​ξ2andtr⁡(A)=ν​α+ε∼(ν+1)​ξ2.\Delta\sim-4\xi^{2}\quad\text{and}\quad\rm tr(A)=\nu\alpha+\varepsilon\sim(\nu+1)\xi^{2}.

Therefore, there exists δm>0\delta_{m}>0 such that for ξ\xi in [−δm,δm][-\delta_{m},\delta_{m}], Δ≤0\Delta\leq 0 and

12≤tr⁡(A)(ν+1)​ξ2≤2.{1\over 2}\leq\frac{\rm tr(A)}{(\nu+1)\xi^{2}}\leq 2.

(3.2) then follows promptly from (2.12).

Now, for any initial data Y0Y_{0} with supp​(Y^0)⊂[−δm,δm]\text{supp}(\widehat{Y}_{0})\subset[-\delta_{m},\delta_{m}],

E⁡(t)=∫|ξ|≤δm|Y^​(t,ξ)|2​dξ≤C​∫exp⁡(−2​β​t​ξ2)​dξ​(supξ(|Y0^​(ξ)|2))≤Ct−1/2∥Y0∥2Lx1,\begin{split}E(t)&=\int_{|\xi|\leq\delta_{m}}|\widehat{Y}(t,\xi)|^{2}d\xi\leq C\int\exp(-2\beta t\xi^{2})d\xi(\sup_{\xi}(|\widehat{Y_{0}}(\xi)|^{2}))\\ &\leq Ct^{-1/2}\|Y_{0}\|^{2}_{L_{x}^{1}},\end{split}

by using the change of variable τ=2​β​t​ξ\tau=\sqrt{2\beta t}\xi. □\square

3.2. High frequency analysis

The complete dissipation and the partial dissipation cases have to be studied separately. In the latter case, we will give one example where the decay rate can be arbitrarily small.

Introducing the number

{r}={1,if ​r≠0,0,if ​r=0,\{r\}=\begin{cases}1,&\quad\text{if }r\not=0,\\ 0,&\quad\text{if }r=0,\end{cases}

for r∈ℝr\in\mathbb{R}. Then order​(σ)={a}+{c}−{b}−{d}\text{order}(\sigma)=\{a\}+\{c\}-\{b\}-\{d\} and order​(ε)=2−2​{d}\text{order}(\varepsilon)=2-2\{d\}.

3.2.1. The complete dissipation case (ν=1\nu=1).

It is observed in the following that order(σ)(\sigma) dictates if the system is in the KdV-Burgers class or in the BBM-Burgers class.

Proposition 3.3.

Assume ν=1\nu=1. For any δ>0\delta>0, there exists β>0\beta>0, such that if supp​(Y^0)⊂ℝ\[−δ,δ]\text{supp}(\widehat{Y}_{0})\subset\mathbb{R}\backslash[-\delta,\delta],

(3.3) E⁡(t)≤exp⁡(−2​β​t)​‖Y0‖Lx22,E(t)\leq\exp(-2\beta t)\|Y_{0}\|^{2}_{L^{2}_{x}},

for any t>0t>0. In addition,

  • •

    if order​(σ)≤0\text{order}(\sigma)\leq 0, the system is in the BBM–Burgers class. Namely, there exist positive constants δM,β\delta_{M},\beta and CC, such that for |ξ|>δM|\xi|>\delta_{M} and t>0t>0,

    ‖exp⁡(−t​A)‖≤C​e−β​t;\|\exp(-tA)\|\leq Ce^{-\beta t};
  • •

    if order​(σ)≥1\text{order}(\sigma)\geq 1, the system is in the KdV–Burgers class. Namely, there exist positive constants δM,β\delta_{M},\beta and CC, such that for |ξ|>δM|\xi|>\delta_{M} and t>0t>0,

    ‖exp⁡(−t​A)‖≤C​e−β​ξ2​t.\|\exp(-tA)\|\leq Ce^{-\beta\xi^{2}t}.

Proof.  ¿From (2.3), one finds that for ξ\xi almost everywhere,

12​dd​t​|Y^​(t,ξ)|2+α⁡(ξ)​|η^​(t,ξ)|2+ε⁡(ξ)​|w^​(t,ξ)|2=0.{1\over 2}{d\over dt}|\widehat{Y}(t,\xi)|^{2}+\alpha(\xi)|\widehat{\eta}(t,\xi)|^{2}+\varepsilon(\xi)|\widehat{w}(t,\xi)|^{2}=0.

This gives directly, by setting β=min⁡{α⁡(δ),ε⁡(δ)}\beta=\min\{\alpha(\delta),\varepsilon(\delta)\} which is positive, that (3.3) is valid. Furthermore, ‖exp⁡(−t​A)‖≤C​e−β​t\|\exp(-tA)\|\leq Ce^{-\beta t} for |ξ|>δ|\xi|>\delta. To figure out if the system is in the BBM-Burgers or in the KdV-Burgers class, we separate the cases as follows.

  • •

    Assume first order​(σ)≥1\text{order}(\sigma)\geq 1. Then either d=0d=0 or b=0b=0. Without loss of generality, let us assume d=0d=0.

    • –

      If Δ=(α−ε)2−4​ξ2​σ2>0\Delta=(\alpha-\varepsilon)^{2}-4\xi^{2}\sigma^{2}>0 for |ξ||\xi| large enough, then order​(σ)=1\text{order}(\sigma)=1. In that case, there exist β>0\beta>0 and δM>0\delta_{M}>0

      λ1≥det(A)tr⁡(A)=α+σ2αξ2+1≥2​β​ξ2\lambda_{1}\geq\frac{\det(A)}{\rm tr(A)}=\frac{\alpha+\sigma^{2}}{\frac{\alpha}{\xi^{2}}+1}\geq 2\beta\xi^{2}

      for |ξ|>δM|\xi|>\delta_{M}. By using (2.13)

      ‖exp⁡(−t​A)‖≤C⁡(1+t​ξ2)​e−2​β​t​ξ2≤C​e−β​t​ξ2\|\exp(-tA)\|\leq C(1+t\xi^{2})e^{-2\beta t\xi^{2}}\leq Ce^{-{\beta}t\xi^{2}}

      for |ξ|>δM|\xi|>\delta_{M} and the system is in the KdV-Burgers class.

    • –

      If Δ≤0\Delta\leq 0 for |ξ||\xi| large enough, then there exists δM>0\delta_{M}>0 such that for |ξ|>δM|\xi|>\delta_{M}, 12​ξ2≤tr⁡(A)≤2​ξ2{1\over 2}\xi^{2}\leq\rm tr(A)\leq 2\xi^{2}, and (2.12) implies that the system is in the KdV-Burgers class.

  • •

    Assume now that order​(σ)≤0\text{order}(\sigma)\leq 0.

    • –

      If b≠0b\neq 0 and d≠0d\neq 0 (weakly dispersive systems) then for |ξ||\xi| large enough, Re⁡(λ1)≤tr⁡(A)∼1b+1d{\rm Re}(\lambda_{1})\leq\rm tr(A)\sim\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{d} as |ξ|→∞|\xi|\rightarrow\infty. This shows that a damping like e−β​t​ξ2e^{-\beta t\xi^{2}} is unlikely for high frequencies. Therefore the weakly dispersive systems are in the BBM-Burgers class.

    • –

      if (b≠0b\neq 0 and d=0d=0) or (b=0b=0 and d≠0d\neq 0). Without loss of generality, let us consider the case b≠0b\neq 0 and d=0d=0. Since Δ∼ξ4\Delta\sim\xi^{4} as |ξ|→∞|\xi|\to\infty, we have

      λ1≤2​det(A)tr⁡(A)=2​(α+σ2)αξ2+1∼C=O⁡(1)\lambda_{1}\leq\frac{2\det(A)}{\rm tr(A)}=\frac{2(\alpha+\sigma^{2})}{\frac{\alpha}{\xi^{2}}+1}\sim C=O(1)

      as |ξ|→∞|\xi|\to\infty. This shows that a damping like e−β​t​ξ2e^{-\beta t\xi^{2}} is again unlikely for high frequencies. Therefore the system is in the BBM-Burgers class.

□\square

3.2.2. The partial dissipation case (ν=0\nu=0).

We first note that when a system satisfies (C2) hypothesis, σ=0\sigma=0 and therefore λ1=0\lambda_{1}=0 at ξ=a−12\xi=a^{-{1\over 2}}. But one can always chose δM{\delta_{M}} large enough so for |ξ|>δM|\xi|>{\delta_{M}}, σ\sigma is positive, bounded from below and away from zero. Therefore the point where σ\sigma vanishes will be considered in the next subsection. We now prove that in the partial dissipation case, the decay rate is related to order​(σ)\text{order}(\sigma) and the strength of the dissipation which is characterized by order​(ε)\text{order}(\varepsilon).

Proposition 3.4.

With ν=0\nu=0,

  • •

    if order(σ)≥2−12(\sigma)\geq 2-\frac{1}{2}order(ε)(\varepsilon), then the system is in the KdV-Burgers class;

  • •

    if ||order(σ)|<2−12(\sigma)|<2-\frac{1}{2}order(ε)(\varepsilon), then the system is in the BBM-Burgers class.
    In above two cases, when Y^0\widehat{Y}_{0} is supported in ℝ\[−δM,δM]\mathbb{R}\backslash[-{\delta_{M}},{\delta_{M}}], then for any t>0t>0,

    E⁡(t)≤C​exp⁡(−2​β​t)​‖Y0‖Lx22;E(t)\leq C\exp(-2\beta t)\|Y_{0}\|^{2}_{L^{2}_{x}};

    if order(σ)≤−2+12(\sigma)\leq-2+\frac{1}{2}order(ε)(\varepsilon), arbitrarily slow decay can occur.

(3.4) 2​λ1=ε⁡(1−(1−4​ξ2​σ2ε2)1/2)2\lambda_{1}=\varepsilon\left(1-\left(1-{4\xi^{2}\sigma^{2}\over\varepsilon^{2}}\right)^{1/2}\right)

which is a direct consequence of (2.8).

    When order(ε)(\varepsilon)=0, i.e d≠0d\neq 0 (and order​(σ)≤1\text{order}(\sigma)\leq 1):

    • –

      if order​(σ)≥−1\text{order}(\sigma)\geq-1, and if Δ=ε2−4​ξ2​σ2>0\Delta=\varepsilon^{2}-4\xi^{2}\sigma^{2}>0 for |ξ||\xi| large enough, which is possible only for order​(σ)=−1\text{order}(\sigma)=-1, we have

      λ1≥det(A)tr⁡(A)≥C​ξ2​σ2=O⁡(1)\lambda_{1}\geq\frac{\det(A)}{\rm tr(A)}\geq C\xi^{2}\sigma^{2}=O(1)

      as |ξ|→∞|\xi|\to\infty. Then by (2.13) we have

      ‖e−t​A‖≤C⁡(1+t​|ξ|​σ)​e−t​λ1≤C​e−β​t\|e^{-tA}\|\leq C(1+t|\xi|\sigma)e^{-t\lambda_{1}}\leq Ce^{-\beta t}

      for |ξ||\xi| large enough and the system is in the BBM-Burgers class. On the other hand, if Δ≤0\Delta\leq 0 for high frequencies, since tr⁡(A)∼1d\rm tr(A)\sim\frac{1}{d} as |ξ|→∞|\xi|\rightarrow\infty, then (2.12) implies that the system is in the BBM-Burgers class;

    • –

      if order​(σ)=−2\text{order}(\sigma)=-2, Δ∼1d2>0\Delta\sim\frac{1}{d^{2}}>0 as |ξ|→∞|\xi|\rightarrow\infty and by (3.4), λ1∼C​|ξ|−2\lambda_{1}\sim C|\xi|^{-2}, therefore arbitrarily slow decay could occur. An example of such case will be given below.

  • •

    When order​(ε)=2\text{order}(\varepsilon)=2 i.e d=0d=0 (and order​(σ)≥−1\text{order}(\sigma)\geq-1): Δ=ξ2​(ξ2−4​σ2)\Delta=\xi^{2}(\xi^{2}-4\sigma^{2}) has a limit Δ0\Delta_{0} in [−∞,+∞][-\infty,+\infty] when |ξ||\xi| approaches +∞+\infty.

    • –

      If Δ0\Delta_{0} is in (−∞,0](-\infty,0], then since tr⁡(A)=ξ2\rm tr(A)=\xi^{2}, (2.12) implies that the system is in the KdV-Burgers class. This occurs when order​(σ)=2\text{order}(\sigma)=2 and may occur when order​(σ)=1\text{order}(\sigma)=1.

    • –

      If Δ0\Delta_{0} is in (0,+∞](0,+\infty], then since

      2​det(A)tr⁡(A)≥λ1≥det(A)tr⁡(A)=σ2,\frac{2\det(A)}{\rm tr(A)}\geq\lambda_{1}\geq\frac{\det(A)}{\rm tr(A)}=\sigma^{2},

      (2.13) implies for any ξ\xi

      (3.5) ‖exp⁡(−t​A)‖≤C⁡(1+|ξ|​σ​min⁡(t,1Δ))​exp⁡(−t​σ2).\|\exp(-tA)\|\leq C\left(1+|\xi|\sigma\min\left(t,\frac{1}{\sqrt{\Delta}}\right)\right)\exp(-t\sigma^{2}).
      • *

        If order​(σ)=1\text{order}(\sigma)=1, then (3.5) implies the system is in the KdV-Burgers class.

        If order​(σ)=0\text{order}(\sigma)=0, |ξ​σ|Δ=0​(1)\frac{|\xi\sigma|}{\sqrt{\Delta}}=0(1) as |ξ|→∞|\xi|\rightarrow\infty, the system is in the BBM-Burgers class. And similarly,

Example of slow decay: Consider the linearized BBM-BBM system with partial dissipation,

ηt+ux−b​ηx​x​t=0,ut+ηx−d​ux​x​t=ux​x,\begin{split}&\eta_{t}+u_{x}-b\eta_{xxt}=0,\\ &u_{t}+\eta_{x}-du_{xxt}=u_{xx},\end{split}

Δ∼1d>0,|z|=2|ξ|σ∼2b​d1|ξ|,2​λ1=tr⁡(A)​(1−(1−4​det(A)(tr⁡(A))2)1/2)∼ 2​det(A)tr⁡(A)∼2d​ξ2.\begin{split}\Delta&\sim{1\over d}>0,\quad|z|=\displaystyle{2|\xi|\sigma\sim{2\over\sqrt{bd}}\ {1\over|\xi|}},\\ 2\lambda_{1}&=\rm tr(A)\left(1-\left(1-{4\det(A)\over(\rm tr(A))^{2}}\right)^{1/2}\right)\sim\ 2\ {\det(A)\over\rm tr(A)}\sim{2\over d\xi^{2}}.\end{split}

‖e−t​A‖≤C​exp⁡(−β​tξ2)\displaystyle\|e^{-tA}\|\leq C\exp\left(-{\beta t\over\xi^{2}}\right)

which shows that any arbitrary slow decay could occur.

3.3. Middle range frequency analysis

We first note from Lemma 2.7 that to get the optimal decay estimate for the cases where det(A)\det(A) (and therefore λ1\lambda_{1}) has a zero for |ξ|>0|\xi|>0, these cases need to be discussed separately. Therefore, we have the following two propositions.

Proposition 3.5.

Assume that ν=1\nu=1, or that ν=0\nu=0 and the dispersive coefficients a,b,c,da,b,c,d satisfy (C1). Then for any δm\delta_{m} and δM\delta_{M}, 0<δm≤δM0<\delta_{m}\leq\delta_{M}, there exists β>0\beta>0 such that for |ξ|∈[δm,δM]|\xi|\in[\delta_{m},\delta_{M}] and for any t>0t>0,

(3.6) ‖exp⁡(−t​A)‖≤C​exp⁡(−β​t).\|\exp(-tA)\|\leq C\exp(-\beta t).

Moreover for any Y0^\widehat{Y_{0}} with support included in [δm,δM]∪[−δM,−δm][\delta_{m},\delta_{M}]\cup[-\delta_{M},-\delta_{m}],

E⁡(t)≤C​exp⁡(−2​β​t)​‖Y0‖Lx22.E(t)\leq C\exp(-2\beta t)||Y_{0}||^{2}_{L_{x}^{2}}.

Proof.  Since tr⁡(A)\rm tr{(A)} and det(A)\det(A) cannot vanish for |ξ|∈[δm,δM]|\xi|\in[\delta_{m},\delta_{M}] under the assumptions, (3.6) is the direct consequence of (2.12) and (2.13). In addition

E⁡(t)≤supξ‖e−t​A‖2​‖Y0^‖Lξ22≤C​exp⁡(−2​β​t)||Y0||Lx22,E(t)\leq\sup_{\xi}||e^{-tA}||^{2}\,||\widehat{Y_{0}}||^{2}_{L^{2}_{\xi}}\leq C\exp(-2\beta t)||Y_{0}||^{2}_{L_{x}^{2}},

which completes the proof of the proposition. □\square

Remark 3.6.

By noticing that (3.6) can be replaced by

‖exp⁡(−t​A)‖≤C​exp⁡(−β∗​t​ξ2).\|\exp(-tA)\|\leq C\exp(-\beta^{*}t\xi^{2}).

with β∗=β/δM2\beta^{*}=\beta/\delta_{M}^{2}, the middle range frequency analysis and the high frequency analysis can be combined to simplify certain calculations for these systems regardless if they are in BBM-Burgers class or KdV-Burgers class.

Proposition 3.7.

Assume that ν=0\nu=0 and the dispersive coefficients satisfy (C2). Then for any 0<δm<δM0<\delta_{m}<\delta_{M} with r=a−12∈[δm,δM]r=a^{-{1\over 2}}\in[\delta_{m},\delta_{M}], there exists β>0\beta>0 and C>0C>0 such that for any |ξ|∈[δm,δM]|\xi|\in[\delta_{m},\delta_{M}] and for any t>0t>0,

(3.7) ∥exp(−tA)∥≤Cexp{−βt(|ξ|−r)2)}.\|\exp(-tA)\|\leq C{\rm exp}\{-\beta t(|\xi|-r)^{2})\}.

Moreover for any Y0^\widehat{Y_{0}} with support included in [δm,δM]∪[−δM,−δm][\delta_{m},\delta_{M}]\cup[-\delta_{M},-\delta_{m}] and for any t>0t>0,

E(t)≤Ct−1/2||Y0||Lx12.E(t)\leq Ct^{-1/2}||Y_{0}||^{2}_{L_{x}^{1}}.
Remark 3.8.

Proposition 3.7 shows that even when the dichotomy is not valid, the energy could decay as O(t−1/4)(t^{-1/4}) when tt goes to +∞+\infty.

Proof.  Since det(A)\det(A) vanishes at r=(a)−1r=(\sqrt{a})^{-1} and, when |ξ|→r|\xi|\to r, Δ∼aa+d>0\Delta\sim\frac{a}{a+d}>0, λ1∼β​det​(A)∼β​σ2∼β​(|ξ|−r)2\lambda_{1}\sim\beta{\rm det}(A)\sim\beta\sigma^{2}\sim\beta(|\xi|-r)^{2}. Therefore, from (2.13),

‖exp⁡(−t​A)‖≤C⁡(1+min⁡(t,1)​σ)​exp​(−β​σ2​t)\|\exp(-tA)\|\leq C(1+\min(t,1)\sigma){\rm exp}(-\beta\sigma^{2}t)

as |ξ||\xi| in the neighborhood of rr. Using the fact that for t>0t>0, min⁡(t,1)≤t\min(t,1)\leq\sqrt{t}, so there exists C>0C>0 such that

‖exp⁡(−t​A)‖≤C⁡(1+t​σ)​exp​(−β​σ2​t)≤C​exp​(−β2​σ2​t),\|\exp(-tA)\|\leq C(1+\sqrt{t}\sigma){\rm exp}(-\beta\sigma^{2}t)\leq C{\rm exp}(-\frac{\beta}{2}\sigma^{2}t),

we obtain the estimate (3.7) for |ξ||\xi| close to rr. For other |ξ||\xi| in [δm,δM][\delta_{m},\delta_{M}], the same argument in the proof of Proposition 3.5 and Remark 3.6 applies. For the decay rate of E⁡(t)E(t), same argument as in the proof of Propositions 3.2 can be used. In fact, |ξ|−r|\xi|-r plays the same role as |ξ||\xi| in that case. □\square

3.4. Decay for linear systems

Since linear system (1.3) defines a semi-group e−t​Ae^{-tA} for t≥0t\geq 0, that is contracting on L2×L2L^{2}\times L^{2} in the variable (η,w)(\eta,w), the initial value problem is therefore well-posed and the L2L^{2} norm decays.

Combining the low, middle and high frequency analysis, the decay rate for the linear system (1.3) can be stated as

Theorem 3.9.

For systems (1.3) with the dispersive constants a,b,c,da,b,c,d satisfy the constraints (C0)-(C1) or (C0)-(C2), assuming either {ν=1}\{\nu=1\} or, {ν=0\{\nu=0 and order(σ)>−2+12order(ε)}\text{order}(\sigma)>-2+\frac{1}{2}\text{order}(\varepsilon)\}, then for any (η0,H​u0)=(η0,w0)∈(L1​(ℝ)∩L2​(ℝ))2(\eta_{0},Hu_{0})=(\eta_{0},w_{0})\in(L^{1}(\mathbb{R})\cap L^{2}(\mathbb{R}))^{2} where H^​u^0=((1−a​ξ2)​(1+d​ξ2)(1−c​ξ2)​(1+b​ξ2))12​u^0\widehat{H}\widehat{u}_{0}=(\frac{(1-a\xi^{2})(1+d\xi^{2})}{(1-c\xi^{2})(1+b\xi^{2})})^{1\over 2}\widehat{u}_{0}, there exists a constant CC, such that for any t>0t>0

∥(η,Hu)∥Lx2=∥(η,w)∥Lx2≤Ct−1/4.\|(\eta,Hu)\|_{L_{x}^{2}}=\|(\eta,w)\|_{L_{x}^{2}}\leq Ct^{-1/4}.
Remark 3.10.

This is equivalent to say , with respect to physical variables (η,u)(\eta,u), that for any (η0,u0)∈(Lx2∩Lx1)×(Hxh∩Wxh,1)(\eta_{0},u_{0})\in(L_{x}^{2}\cap L^{1}_{x})\times(H_{x}^{h}\cap W_{x}^{h,1}),

∥(η,u)∥Lx2×Hxh≤Ct−1/4\|(\eta,u)\|_{L_{x}^{2}\times H_{x}^{h}}\leq Ct^{-1/4}

for any t>0t>0, where h=order​(H^)={a}+{d}−{c}−{b}h=\text{order}(\widehat{H})=\{a\}+\{d\}-\{c\}-\{b\}.

Proof.  Combining the low, middle and high frequency analysis, we have

E⁡(t)=El​o​w​(t)+Em​i​d​d​l​e​(t)+Eh​i​g​h​(t)≤C⁡(η0,u0)​(t−12+e−2​β​t)E(t)=E_{low}(t)+E_{middle}(t)+E_{high}(t)\leq C(\eta_{0},u_{0})(t^{-{1\over 2}}+e^{-2\beta t})

for t>0t>0 where C⁡(η0,u0)C(\eta_{0},u_{0}) is a function of the dispersive coefficients and the norms of η0\eta_{0} and u0u_{0}. □\square

We complete this section by the following

Corollary 3.11.

For any dissipation, the classical Boussinesq system, the Bona–Smith system, the coupled KdV–BBM (b=c=0b=c=0) system, the BBM–KdV systems (a=d=0a=d=0) and the weakly dispersive systems (b>0b>0 and d>0d>0) with a<0a<0 or c<0c<0 belong to the BBM–Burgers class.

Corollary 3.12.

With complete dissipation, the KdV–KdV system (b=d=0b=d=0, a=c>0a=c>0) belongs to the KdV–Burgers class; the weakly dispersive systems (b>0b>0 and d>0d>0) belong to the BBM–Burgers class.

Remark 3.13.

When the consideration is restricted to the linear systems, a result similar to Theorem 3.9 (substituting α\alpha for ε\varepsilon in the statement) holds when one replaces (ν​ηx​x,ux​x)(\nu\eta_{xx},u_{xx}) by (ηx​x,ν​ux​x)(\eta_{xx},\nu u_{xx}) in the right-hand side of (2.1) since η\eta and uu play the same role.

4. Nonlinear Theory

For convenience, we will only consider in this section (i) the complete dissipation and (ii) the partial dissipation with a,b,c,da,b,c,d satisfy the (C1) assumption. The partial dissipation with a,b,c,da,b,c,d satisfy (C2) will be considered elsewhere.

4.1. A general result

Consider an evolution equation that reads

(4.1) vt+L​v+∂x(F⁡(v))=0,v⁡(t=0)=v0v_{t}+Lv+\partial_{x}(F(v))=0,\quad v(t=0)=v_{0}

where LL is a linear unbounded operator with symbol AA and FF is a nonlinear quadratic operator.

Assuming that LL generates a semi–group S⁡(t)S(t) on Lx2L^{2}_{x} that satisfies the dichotomy assumption (3.1), namely there exist β>0\beta>0 and δ>0\delta>0 (δ\delta can be +∞+\infty) such that for any t>0t>0 and

(4.2) ∙ for |ξ|≤δ,∥S(t)∥≤Cexp(−βtξ2),∙ for |ξ|>δ,∥S(t)∥≤Cexp(−βt).\begin{split}\bullet&\text{ for }|\xi|\leq\delta,\ \|S(t)\|\leq C\exp(-\beta t\xi^{2}),\\ \bullet&\text{ for }|\xi|>\delta,\ \|S(t)\|\leq C\exp(-\beta t).\end{split}

In addition,

(4.3) supt≥0(t1/4​‖S⁡(t)​v0‖Lx2)≤C1​‖v0‖Lx1∩Lx2=C¯.\sup_{t\geq 0}(t^{1/4}\|S(t)v_{0}\|_{L^{2}_{x}})\leq C_{1}\|v_{0}\|_{L_{x}^{1}\cap L_{x}^{2}}=\overline{C}.

Assuming also the nonlinear term F⁡(v)F(v) satisfies

(4.4) sup|ξ|≤δ|F^|+(∫|ξ|≥δ|ξ|2​|F^|2​𝑑ξ)1/2≤C​‖v‖Lx22\sup_{|\xi|\leq\delta}|\widehat{F}|+\left(\int_{|\xi|\geq\delta}|\xi|^{2}|\widehat{F}|^{2}d\xi\right)^{1/2}\leq C\|v\|^{2}_{L^{2}_{x}}

for any t>0t>0, where F^=ℱ⁡(F⁡(v))\widehat{F}=\mathcal{F}(F(v)).

Let us recall that a mild solution to (4.1) is a solution to the integral equation

(4.5) v⁡(t)=S⁡(t)​v0−∫0tS⁡(t−s)​∂xF⁡(v⁡(s))​𝑑s.v(t)=S(t)v_{0}-\int_{0}^{t}S(t-s)\partial_{x}F(v(s))ds.

Under the above assumptions, we may construct a solution to (4.5) by performing a fixed point argument (see [10], [14], [6], [11]) on the space

E={u:supt>0{t1/4​‖u⁡(t)‖Lx²}<∞},E=\left\{u:\ \sup_{t>0}\{t^{1/4}\|u(t)\|_{L^{\texttwosuperior}_{x}}\}<\infty\right\},

which is a Banach space of functions that are continuous in time with value in L2L^{2} that are O(t−1/4)O(t^{-1/4}) when tt goes to +∞+\infty. If C¯\overline{C} is small enough, a fixed point argument to the Duhamel’s form of the equation in the ball in EE centered at origin would provide the solution.

Theorem 4.1.

For system (4.1) with assumptions (4.2)-(4.3)-(4.4), there exists a numerical constant CC such that for any mild solution to (4.1) starting from v0v_{0} with

‖v0‖Lx1∩Lx2≤C,\|v_{0}\|_{L_{x}^{1}\cap L^{2}_{x}}\leq C,

then

(4.6) ∥v(t)∥Lx2≤O(t−1/4)ast→∞.\|v(t)\|_{L^{2}_{x}}\leq O(t^{-1/4})\quad\text{as}\quad t\rightarrow\infty.

Proof.  To begin, we first control the low frequency part of the nonlinear term. Let

N^:=ℱ⁡(∫0tS⁡(t−s)​∂xF⁡(v⁡(s))​ds)=i​∫0te−(t−s)​A​ξ​F^​(v⁡(s))​𝑑s.\begin{split}\widehat{N}&:={\mathcal{F}}\left(\int_{0}^{t}S(t-s)\partial_{x}F(v(s))ds\right)\\ &=i\int_{0}^{t}e^{-(t-s)A}\xi\widehat{F}(v(s))ds.\end{split}

Using the first inequality in (4.2) in combination with (4.4), one obtains

(4.7) (∫|ξ|≤δ|N^|2​𝑑ξ)1/2≤C​∫0t[∫|ξ|≤δ‖e−(t−s)​A‖2​ξ2​|F^|2​𝑑ξ]1/2​𝑑s≤C​∫0t[∫ℝξ2​e−2​β​(t−s)​ξ2​𝑑ξ]1/2​(sup|ξ|≤δ|F^|)​𝑑s≤C​∫0t‖v⁡(s)‖Lx22(t−s)3/4​ds.\begin{split}&\left(\int_{|\xi|\leq\delta}|\widehat{N}|^{2}d\xi\right)^{1/2}\leq C\int_{0}^{t}\left[\int_{|\xi|\leq\delta}\|e^{-(t-s)A}\|^{2}\xi^{2}|\widehat{F}|^{2}d\xi\right]^{1/2}ds\\ &\hskip 14.22636pt\leq C\int_{0}^{t}\left[\int_{\mathbb{R}}\xi^{2}e^{-2\beta(t-s)\xi^{2}}d\xi\right]^{1/2}\left(\sup_{|\xi|\leq\delta}|\widehat{F}|\right)ds\\ &\hskip 14.22636pt\leq C\int_{0}^{t}{\|v(s)\|^{2}_{L^{2}_{x}}\over(t-s)^{3/4}}\ ds.\end{split}

We now control the high frequency part of the nonlinear term, using the second inequality in (4.2) in combination with (4.4)

(4.8) (∫|ξ|≥δ|N^|2​𝑑ξ)1/2≤C​∫0te−β⁡(t−s)​(∫|ξ|>δξ2​|F^|2​𝑑ξ)1/2​𝑑s≤C​∫0te−β⁡(t−s)​‖v⁡(s)‖Lx22​ds.\begin{split}\left(\int_{|\xi|\geq\delta}|\widehat{N}|^{2}d\xi\right)^{1/2}&\leq C\int_{0}^{t}e^{-\beta(t-s)}\left(\int_{|\xi|>\delta}\xi^{2}|\widehat{F}|^{2}d\xi\right)^{1/2}ds\\ &\leq C\int_{0}^{t}e^{-\beta(t-s)}\|v(s)\|^{2}_{L^{2}_{x}}ds.\end{split}

Introducing the norm

(4.9) M⁡(t)=sups∈[0,t](s1/4​‖v⁡(s)‖Lx2),M(t)=\sup_{s\in[0,t]}(s^{1/4}\|v(s)\|_{L^{2}_{x}}),

and if vv solves (4.5), then due to (4.7)–(4.8),

t1/4​‖v⁡(t)‖Lx2≤t1/4​‖S⁡(t)​v0‖Lx2+t1/4​‖N^​(t)‖Lξ2≤t1/4​‖S⁡(t)​v0‖Lx2+C​M​(t)2​∫0t[t1/4s1/2​(t−s)3/4+t1/4s1/2​exp⁡(−β⁡(t−s))]​ds.\begin{split}&t^{1/4}\|v(t)\|_{L^{2}_{x}}\leq t^{1/4}\|S(t)v_{0}\|_{L^{2}_{x}}+t^{1/4}\|\hat{N}(t)\|_{L_{\xi}^{2}}\\ &\leq t^{1/4}\|S(t)v_{0}\|_{L^{2}_{x}}+CM(t)^{2}\int_{0}^{t}\left[{t^{1/4}\over s^{1/2}(t-s)^{3/4}}+{t^{1/4}\over s^{1/2}}\exp(-\beta(t-s))\right]ds.\end{split}

By applying the change of variable s=τ​ts=\tau t in the integration, one finds

∫0t[t1/4s1/2​(t−s)3/4+t1/4s1/2​exp⁡(−β⁡(t−s))]​𝑑s≤C+∫01t3/4τ12​exp⁡(−β​t​(1−τ))​dτ≤C.\begin{split}&\int_{0}^{t}\left[{t^{1/4}\over s^{1/2}(t-s)^{3/4}}+{t^{1/4}\over s^{1/2}}\exp(-\beta(t-s))\right]ds\\ \leq&C+\int_{0}^{1}\frac{t^{3/4}}{\tau^{1\over 2}}\exp(-\beta t(1-\tau))d\tau\leq C.\end{split}

Therefore, using the property (4.3), the positive, nondecreasing function M⁡(t)M(t) satisfies M⁡(0)=0M(0)=0 and for any t≥0t\geq 0,

(4.10) C0​M​(t)2−M⁡(t)+C¯≥0,C_{0}M(t)^{2}-M(t)+\overline{C}\geq 0,

where C0C_{0} is a positive constant. Choosing C¯\overline{C} such that C0​x2−x+C¯=0C_{0}x^{2}-x+\overline{C}=0 has two real roots 0<r1<r20<r_{1}<r_{2}, namely choosing C¯<14​C0\overline{C}<\frac{1}{4C_{0}}, then (4.10) holds only if M⁡(t)M(t) is trapped in the interval [0,r1][0,r_{1}]. Therefore when

‖v0‖Lx1∩Lx2≤C¯C1<14​C0​C1\|v_{0}\|_{L_{x}^{1}\cap L_{x}^{2}}\leq\frac{\overline{C}}{C_{1}}<\frac{1}{4C_{0}C_{1}}

M⁡(t)M(t) is bounded and (4.6) is valid. □\square

4.2. Applications to weakly dispersive systems with complete dissipation or partial dissipation

Since b>0b>0 and d>0d>0, order​(σ)≤0\text{order}(\sigma)\leq 0 and the corresponding linearized system is in the BBM-Burgers class. From Proposition 3.3 and Proposition • ‣ 3.4, this corresponds to consider complete dissipation, or partial dissipation together with order​(σ)≥−1\text{order}(\sigma)\geq-1.

Theorem 4.2.

Consider a weakly dispersive two–way wave model (b>0​ and ​d>0)(b>0\text{ and }d>0) with either the complete dissipation or the partial dissipation together with a<0a<0 or c<0c<0. Then, for small initial data,

  • •

    if HH is of order 0,

    (4.11) ∥η(t)∥Lx22+∥u(t)∥Lx22≤O(t−1/2);\|\eta(t)\|^{2}_{L^{2}_{x}}+\|u(t)\|^{2}_{L^{2}_{x}}\leq O(t^{-1/2});
  • •

    if HH is of order 1,

    (4.12) ∥η(t)∥Lx22+∥u(t)∥Hx12≤O(t−1/2);\|\eta(t)\|^{2}_{L^{2}_{x}}+\|u(t)\|^{2}_{H^{1}_{x}}\leq O(t^{-1/2});
  • •

    if HH is of order −1-1,

    (4.13) ∥η(t)∥Hx12+∥u(t)∥Lx22≤O(t−1/2);\|\eta(t)\|^{2}_{H^{1}_{x}}+\|u(t)\|^{2}_{L^{2}_{x}}\leq O(t^{-1/2});

as t→∞t\to\infty.

Proof.  Note that the theorem is proved after (4.4) is validated and we will do that by discussing the cases according to the order of HH.

  • •

    If HH is of order 0 or 1. Introducing the change of variable

    v=ℱ−1​(η^,H^​u^)=ℱ−1​(η^,w^),v=\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\widehat{\eta},\widehat{H}\widehat{u})=\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\widehat{\eta},\widehat{w}),

    the full nonlinear system

    (4.14) ηt+ux+a​ux​x​x−b​ηx​x​t+(η​u)x=ν​ηx​x,ut+ηx+c​ηx​x​x−d​ux​x​t+u​ux=ux​x,\begin{split}&\eta_{t}+u_{x}+au_{xxx}-b\eta_{xxt}+(\eta u)_{x}=\nu\eta_{xx},\\ &u_{t}+\eta_{x}+c\eta_{xxx}-du_{xxt}+uu_{x}=u_{xx},\end{split}

    transforms to

    vt+Lv=−∂xF(v),v_{t}+Lv=-\partial_{x}F(v),

    where LL has symbol A=(ν​αi​sgn​(ω1)​ξ​σi​sgn​(ω2)​ξ​σε)A=\begin{pmatrix}\nu\alpha&i{\rm sgn}(\omega_{1})\xi\sigma\\ i{\rm sgn}(\omega_{2})\xi\sigma&\varepsilon\end{pmatrix} and FF reads

    F⁡(v)=((1−b∂2x)−1ηH−1w12H(1−d∂2x)−1(H−1w)2).F(v)=\begin{pmatrix}(1-b\partial^{2}_{x})^{-1}\eta H^{-1}w\\ \frac{1}{2}H(1-d\partial^{2}_{x})^{-1}(H^{-1}w)^{2}\end{pmatrix}.

    To check (4.4), it is natural to separate the estimate into two parts.

    • –

      Low frequency (|ξ|≤δ|\xi|\leq\delta) estimate: Since H−1H^{-1}, which has order 00 or −1-1, is bounded on Lx2L^{2}_{x}, straightforward computations lead to

      ‖η​H−1​w^‖Lξ∞+‖(H−1​w)2^‖Lξ∞≤C⁡(‖η‖Lx22+‖H−1​w‖Lx22)≤C⁡(‖η‖Lx22+‖w‖Lx22).\begin{split}\|\widehat{\eta H^{-1}w}\|_{L^{\infty}_{\xi}}&+\|\widehat{(H^{-1}w)^{2}}\|_{L^{\infty}_{\xi}}\leq C(\|\eta\|^{2}_{L^{2}_{x}}+\|H^{-1}w\|^{2}_{L^{2}_{x}})\\ &\leq C(\|\eta\|^{2}_{L^{2}_{x}}+\|w\|^{2}_{L^{2}_{x}}).\end{split}

      Because (1−b∂x2)−1(1-b\partial_{x}^{2})^{-1} and H(1−d∂x2)−1H(1-d\partial_{x}^{2})^{-1} are bounded operators,

      sup|ξ|≤δ|F^|≤C​‖v‖Lx22.\sup_{|\xi|\leq\delta}|\widehat{F}|\leq C\|v\|^{2}_{L_{x}^{2}}.
    • –

      High frequency (|ξ|>δ|\xi|>\delta) estimate: Since ∂x(1−b∂x2)−1\partial_{x}(1-b\partial^{2}_{x})^{-1} is a smoothing operator (it is of order −1-1) and H−1H^{-1} is a bounded operator on Lx2L^{2}_{x},

      ∥∂x(1−b∂2x)−1(ηH−1w)∥Lx2≤C∥ηH−1w∥Hx−1≤C​‖η‖Lx2​‖H−1​w‖Lx2≤C⁡(‖η‖Lx22+‖w‖Lx22),\begin{split}&\|\partial_{x}(1-b\partial^{2}_{x})^{-1}(\eta H^{-1}w)\|_{L^{2}_{x}}\leq C\|\eta H^{-1}w\|_{H^{-1}_{x}}\\ &\hskip 14.22636pt\leq C\|\eta\|_{L^{2}_{x}}\|H^{-1}w\|_{L^{2}_{x}}\leq C(\|\eta\|^{2}_{L^{2}_{x}}+\|w\|^{2}_{L^{2}_{x}}),\end{split}

      where Lemma 2.2(ii) in [6],

      ‖f​g‖H−1≤C​‖f‖L2​‖g‖L2\|fg\|_{H^{-1}}\leq C\|f\|_{L^{2}}\|g\|_{L^{2}}

      is used. Now, consider the term ∂x(H(1−d∂x2)−1)((H−1w)2)\partial_{x}(H(1-d\partial^{2}_{x})^{-1})((H^{-1}w)^{2}) in FF. If HH is of order 00, it can be bounded in the same way. If HH is of order 11, then

      ∥∂xH(1−d∂x2)−1(H−1w)2∥Lx2≤C∥(H−1w)2∥Lx2≤C​‖H−1​w‖Hx12≤C​‖w‖Lx22,\begin{split}&\|\partial_{x}H(1-d\partial_{x}^{2})^{-1}(H^{-1}w)^{2}\|_{L^{2}_{x}}\leq C\|(H^{-1}w)^{2}\|_{L^{2}_{x}}\\ &\hskip 14.22636pt\leq C\|H^{-1}w\|^{2}_{H^{1}_{x}}\leq C\|w\|^{2}_{L^{2}_{x}},\end{split}

      where Lemma 2.2(iv) in [6]

      ‖f​g‖L0≤C​‖f‖H1​‖g‖H1\|fg\|_{L^{0}}\leq C\|f\|_{H^{1}}\|g\|_{H^{1}}

      is used.

    Combining the lower frequency and higher frequency analysis, one sees (4.4) is valid and Theorem 4.1 yields the desired result.

  • •

    If HH is of order −1-1, introducing the change of variable

    (4.15) v=ℱ−1​((H−1​η^,u^)).v=\mathcal{F}^{-1}((H^{-1}\widehat{\eta},\widehat{u})).

    and setting τ^=H−1​η^\widehat{\tau}=H^{-1}\widehat{\eta}, the full nonlinear system (4.14) reads

    vt+Lv=−∂xF(v)v_{t}+Lv=-\partial_{x}F(v)

    where LL has symbol A=(ν​αi​sgn​(ω1)​ξ​σi​sgn​(ω2)​ξ​σε)A=\begin{pmatrix}\nu\alpha&i{\rm sgn}(\omega_{1})\xi\sigma\\ i{\rm sgn}(\omega_{2})\xi\sigma&\varepsilon\end{pmatrix} and

    F⁡(v)=(H−1​(1−b​∂2x)−1​(u​H​τ)12(1−d∂2x)−1(u2)).F(v)=\begin{pmatrix}H^{-1}(1-b\partial^{2}x)^{-1}(uH\tau)\\ \frac{1}{2}(1-d\partial^{2}_{x})^{-1}(u^{2})\end{pmatrix}.

    The proof is then very similar to the previous case and therefore omitted.

□\square

Corollary 4.3.

For the following two special cases, we have

  • •

    solutions to Bona–Smith system (a=0,b>0,c<0a=0,b>0,c<0 and d>0d>0) with complete or partial dissipation satisfy (4.13);

  • •

    solutions to BBM–BBM system with complete dissipation (a=c=0,ν=1)a=c=0,\nu=1) satisfy (4.11).

4.3. Application to KdV-Burgers systems with complete dissipation.

Using Proposition 3.3, this implies that order(σ)≥1(\sigma)\geq 1, and then that b=0b=0 and/or d=0d=0.

First case: Consider the case where b=d=0b=d=0. The analysis in [6] implies that a=c=1/6a=c=1/6, so the system satisfies (C2) assumptions. Since the dichotomy assumption (4.2) was proved in Section 3 and the linearized system is in the KdV-Burgers class, Theorem 4.1 applies when (4.4) with δ=+∞\delta=+\infty is verified.

Let us observe that H=1H=1 and that the full nonlinear system reads

vt+Lv=−∂xF(v)v_{t}+Lv=-\partial_{x}F(v)

where v=(η,u)v=(\eta,u), LL has symbol A=(ξ2i​sgn​(ω1)​ξ​σi​sgn​(ω2)​ξ​σξ2)A=\begin{pmatrix}\xi^{2}&i{\rm sgn}(\omega_{1})\xi\sigma\\ i{\rm sgn}(\omega_{2})\xi\sigma&\xi^{2}\end{pmatrix} and

F⁡(v)=(η​uu22).F(v)=\begin{pmatrix}\eta u\\ {u^{2}\over 2}\end{pmatrix}.

Since

‖F⁡(v)‖Lx1≤C⁡(‖η‖Lx22+‖u‖Lx22),\|F(v)\|_{L^{1}_{x}}\leq C(\|\eta\|^{2}_{L^{2}_{x}}+\|u\|^{2}_{L^{2}_{x}}),

(4.4) with δ=∞\delta=\infty is a direct consequence.

Second case: Consider the case where b>0b>0 and d=0d=0. Due to (C0), c≥0c\geq 0. Since order​(σ)≥1\text{order}(\sigma)\geq 1, the system must have a=c>0a=c>0. Therefore order(H)=−1(H)=-1. Introducing the change of variable (4.15) the system reads as (4.3) with the following nonlinearity

F⁡(v)=(H−1​(1−b​∂2x)−1​(u​H​τ)u22).F(v)=\begin{pmatrix}H^{-1}(1-b\partial^{2}x)^{-1}(uH\tau)\\ \frac{u^{2}}{2}\end{pmatrix}.

(4.4) with δ=∞\delta=\infty is valid and the proof is straightforward and then omitted.

Third case: Consider the case where b=0b=0 and d>0d>0. Since order(σ)=1(\sigma)=1, then aa and cc can not vanish and order(H)=1(H)=1. In this case, with the change of variable (• ‣ 4.2), the system reads as (4.3) with FF being

F⁡(v)=(η​H−1​w12H(1−d∂2x)−1(H−1w)2).F(v)=\begin{pmatrix}\eta H^{-1}w\\ \frac{1}{2}H(1-d\partial^{2}_{x})^{-1}(H^{-1}w)^{2}\end{pmatrix}.

(4.4) with δ=∞\delta=\infty is again valid and the proof is straightforward and then omitted.

Therefore we can state

Theorem 4.4.

Consider a KdV-Burgers system with complete dissipation. Then for small initial data,

  • •

    if HH is of order 0,

    (4.16) ∥η(t)∥Lx22+∥u(t)∥Lx22≤O(t−1/2);\|\eta(t)\|^{2}_{L^{2}_{x}}+\|u(t)\|^{2}_{L^{2}_{x}}\leq O(t^{-1/2});
  • •

    if HH is of order 1,

    (4.17) ∥η(t)∥Lx22+∥u(t)∥Hx12≤O(t−1/2);\|\eta(t)\|^{2}_{L^{2}_{x}}+\|u(t)\|^{2}_{H^{1}_{x}}\leq O(t^{-1/2});
  • •

    if HH is of order −1-1,

    (4.18) ∥η(t)∥Hx12+∥u(t)∥Lx22≤O(t−1/2);\|\eta(t)\|^{2}_{H^{1}_{x}}+\|u(t)\|^{2}_{L^{2}_{x}}\leq O(t^{-1/2});

as t→∞t\to\infty.

Remark 4.5.

This is not surprising for KdV-KdV system (b=d=0b=d=0) since if we introduce the new variables η=w1+w2\eta=w^{1}+w^{2} and u=w1−w2u=w^{1}-w^{2}, then (4.14) reads as a system of two linear KdV–Burgers systems (weakly) coupled through nonlinear terms. See Section 2.3 in [6].

4.4. Other cases

In some other cases, the method presented here does not work straightforwardly. As pointed out in the Introduction, other methods exist which might enable the analysis to go further. These methods could also be helpful to extend our local results to global ones.

5. The Lx∞L^{\infty}_{x}–decay rate

First, we observe that for the cases of weakly dispersive wave equations and KdV-KdV system, the nonlinear terms satisfy

(5.1) sup|ξ|≤δ|ξ​F^|+(∫|ξ|>δ|ξ|4​|F^|2​𝑑ξ)1/2≤C​‖v‖Lx2​‖vx‖Lx2.\sup_{|\xi|\leq\delta}|\xi\widehat{F}|+\left(\int_{|\xi|>\delta}|\xi|^{4}|\widehat{F}|^{2}d\xi\right)^{1/2}\leq C\|v\|_{L^{2}_{x}}\|v_{x}\|_{L^{2}_{x}}.

We now estimate the decay rate of ∂xv⁡(t)\partial_{x}v(t) in Lx2L^{2}_{x} when vv solves (4.5). To begin, we differentiate (4.5) with respect to xx and treat the nonlinear term of the resulting equation with a procedure similar to the one in the proof of Theorem 4.1, but using (5.1) instead of (4.4).

We first note that for low frequencies,

(∫|ξ|≤δξ2​|N^|2​𝑑ξ)1/2≤C​∫0t‖v⁡(s)‖Lx2​‖vx​(s)‖Lx2(t−s)3/4​𝑑s\left(\int_{|\xi|\leq\delta}\xi^{2}|\widehat{N}|^{2}d\xi\right)^{1/2}\leq C\int_{0}^{t}{\|v(s)\|_{L^{2}_{x}}\|v_{x}(s)\|_{L^{2}_{x}}\over(t-s)^{3/4}}ds

and for high frequencies

6. Numerical Result

Numerical simulations are performed on several systems and results on BBM-BBM and Bona-Smith systems with complete or partial dissipations are reported here. The results show not only that the theoretical results on the decay rates are sharp, but also the constants involved are reasonably sized.

In these numerical computations, the initial data are taken to be

η0=s​e​c​h2​(22​(x−x0)),u0=η0−η02/4,\begin{split}\eta_{0}&=sech^{2}(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(x-x_{0})),\\ u_{0}&=\eta_{0}-\eta_{0}^{2}/4,\end{split}

where x0x_{0} is in the spatial domain [0,L][0,L], where LL is taken to be large enough so the solution near the boundary is smaller than the machine roundoff error during the whole computation. The spectral method is used on the spatial domain [0,L][0,L] and the leap-frog algorithm is used on the time advancing. The decay rate rr and the constant CC in

‖v‖∼C​t−r, as ​t→∞\|v\|\sim Ct^{-r},\text{ as }t\rightarrow\infty

is calculated by first computing

r⁡(tn):=−log⁡‖v‖​(tn)‖v‖​(tn−1)log⁡tntn−1.r(t_{n}):=-\frac{\log\frac{\|v\|(t_{n})}{\|v\|(t_{n-1})}}{\log\frac{t_{n}}{t_{n-1}}}.

The computation is stopped when r⁡(tn)r(t_{n}) is approaching to a constant and the value rr is obtained by averaging the last 5 data. The constant CC is then computed by averaging the last five ‖v‖​(tn)​tnr\|v\|(t_{n})t_{n}^{r}.

In the computations reported below, L=320L=320, d​x=0.1dx=0.1 and d​t=0.05dt=0.05, where d​xdx and d​tdt are the meshsize in space and time respectively.

BBM-BBM system (a=c=0,b=d=1/6a=c=0,b=d=1/6) with complete dissipation. It is shown in Theorem 4.2 and 5.1 that for small data,

∥v∥L2≤C1t−1/4and∥v∥L∞≤C2t−1/2.\|v\|_{L^{2}}\leq C_{1}t^{-1/4}\quad\text{and}\quad\|v\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C_{2}t^{-1/2}.

The numerical computation is performed for time interval [0,50][0,50], and the result shows

‖v‖L2∼1.4232​t−0.2470and‖v‖L∞∼1.4989​t−0.4963.\|v\|_{L^{2}}\sim 1.4232t^{-0.2470}\quad\text{and}\quad\|v\|_{L^{\infty}}\sim 1.4989t^{-0.4963}.

Therefore, it is clear that the theoretical result is sharp and the constants involved are not large. Moreover, it seems that the small data requirement might be removed if, for example, other methods were employed.

Bona-Smith system (a=0,b=−c=d=1/3a=0,b=-c=d=1/3) with complete and partial dissipation. This case is again covered by Theorem 4.2 and 5.1. By direct computation, we obtain for complete dissipation,

‖v‖L2∼1.4015​t−0.2477,‖v‖L∞∼1.4466​t−0.4998,\|v\|_{L^{2}}\sim 1.4015t^{-0.2477},\quad\|v\|_{L^{\infty}}\sim 1.4466t^{-0.4998},

and for partial dissipation

‖v‖L2∼0.6676​t−0.2519,‖v‖L∞∼0.6595​t−0.5105.\|v\|_{L^{2}}\sim 0.6676t^{-0.2519},\quad\|v\|_{L^{\infty}}\sim 0.6595t^{-0.5105}.
